newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries weighed down in London by Iraq/rate woe.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries weighed down in London by Iraq/rate woe.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries recovered from Tokyo lows but were still reeling in London on Tuesday after a U.S. missile attack on Iraq and a report on possible U.S. monetary tightening damaged investor sentiment, dealers said.
"There's no doubt in the scheme of things we are oversold," said a trader at a Japanese bank in London. "But we seem to be bombarded with new stories."

The U.S. attack sent oil prices higher which was feeding market worries about potential upward pressure on inflation. This was having more impact than any "safe haven" sentiment, and was actually leading to curve flattening rather than steepening.

At the same time, the Wall Street Journal, quoting unnamed Federal Reserve officials, said policy makers were considering a half percentage point interest rate rise as early as this month. The Federal Open Market Committee is to meet on September 24.
The U.S. long bond at 1014 GMT was at 95-10 to yield 7.13 percent, up from 95-04 in Tokyo but down from 95-14 at the New York close on Friday. U.S. markets were shut on Monday.
"In the old days, when this sort of thing (a U.S. military strike) happened, the short end would benefit as money would fly down to the front end," the Japanese bank trader said.
But the Fed report was keeping market players nervous.

Steve Barrow, economist at Chase in London, said the report had had extra impact because the market beforehand had been especially cautious about predicting a large U.S. interest rate rise, having been wrong about Fed policy in recent months.
"A lot of people have been calling for a long time for higher rates and the Fed have not responded," he said.
Subsequently, when economic data supported the Fed's inaction, the market has had to reverse its stance on rates.
"So the market seems loath to really price in too much," Barrow said.
The U.S. military on Tuesday fired 27 long-range cruise missiles against air defence and communications targets in southern Iraq.
October benchmark Brent blend oil futures shot up to $23.50 a barrel overnight, the highest oil price since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait six years ago.
Dealers said two- and five-year paper was most active, but volumes were strong across the board.
The market meanwhile was awaiting the first batch of economic figures in a busy week for U.S. data as the National Association of Purchasing Management report was due at 1400 GMT.
The NAPM was forecast in a Reuter survey to rise to 52.9 in August from 50.2. Barrow said Chase forecast a 55.0 reading.
He said the market expected a bond-negative number after a strong Chicago purchasing managers' index report last week, but he still expected the NAPM result would bruise the market.
December U.S. T-bond futures were at 106-22 in automated trade, down from 106-25 at the previous Chicago close.
Two-year notes were at 99-18 to yield 6.38 percent, against 99-16 in Tokyo and 99-19 in New York. Five-years were at 98-31 to yield 6.75, versus 98-27 in Tokyo and 99-01 in New York.
--Adam Cox, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6784
